items.new: In the first place, the enormous cutting tackles were hoisted up to the main-top. Among other ponderous things, they include a cluster of blocks generally painted green, which no single man can possibly lift; and this vast bunch of grapes was firmly lashed to the lower masthead, the strongest point anywhere above a ship's deck. The end of the hawser-like rope winding through these intricacies was then led to the windlass, and the huge lower block of the tackles was swung over the whale; to this block the great blubber hook, weighing some one hundred pounds, was attached. And now, suspended over the side on stages (planks slung from the ship as platforms), Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, armed with their long spades, began cutting a hole in the body for the insertion of the hook, just above the nearer of the two side-fins. This done, a broad, semicircular line is cut around the hole, the hook is inserted, and the main body of the crew, striking up a wild chorus, now begin heaving in one dense crowd at the windlass. Instantly the entire ship careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frightened mastheads to the sky. More and more she leans over to the whale, while every gasping heave of the windlass is answered by a helping heave from the waves; till at last a swift, startling snap is heard; with a great swash the ship rolls upward and backward from the whale, and the triumphant tackle rises into sight, dragging after it the loosened semicircular end of the first strip of blubber. Now, as the blubber envelops the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so it is stripped off the body precisely as an orange is sometimes peeled — in a spiral. For the strain constantly kept up by the windlass keeps the whale rolling over and over in the water, and the blubber peels off in one even strip along the line called the "scarf," which is cut at the same time by the spades of Starbuck and Stubb, the mates; and just as fast as it is peeled off, and indeed by that very act, it is hoisted higher and higher aloft, until its upper end grazes the main-top. The men at the windlass then stop heaving, and for a moment or two the prodigious, blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky, and everyone present must take good care to dodge it when it swings, or it may box his ears and pitch him headlong overboard.

items.new: In life, the visible surface of the Sperm Whale is not the least among the many marvels he presents. Almost invariably it is obliquely crossed and re-crossed all over with countless straight marks in thick array, something like those in the finest Italian line engravings. But these marks do not seem to be impressed upon the isinglass substance mentioned above; rather, they seem to be seen through it, as if they were engraved upon the body itself. Nor is this all. In some instances, to the quick, observant eye, those linear marks, as in a real engraving, only provide the ground for quite other drawings. These are hieroglyphical; that is, if you call those mysterious ciphers on the walls of pyramids hieroglyphics, then that is the proper word to use here. Remembering well the hieroglyphics on one Sperm Whale in particular, I was much struck by a plate showing the old Indian characters chiseled on the famous hieroglyphic palisades on the banks of the Upper Mississippi. Like those mystic rocks, too, the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable. This allusion to the Indian rocks reminds me of another thing. Besides all the other phenomena that the exterior of the Sperm Whale presents, he quite often shows his back, and more especially his flanks, with the regular linear pattern largely effaced by numerous rough scratches, altogether irregular and random in appearance. I should say that those New England rocks on the sea-coast which Agassiz imagines to bear the marks of violent scraping contact with vast floating icebergs — I should say that those rocks must resemble the Sperm Whale not a little in this respect. It also seems to me that such scratches in the whale are probably made by hostile contact with other whales; for I have noticed them most in the large, full-grown bulls of the species.

items.reason: 'How wonderful it is, then — except after explanation — that...' is a stiff 1851 aside that stops the reader; plain modern form keeps the same hedge.
items.new: A word or two more about this matter of the skin or blubber of the whale. It has already been said that it is stripped from him in long pieces, called blanket-pieces. Like most sea terms, this one is very apt and meaningful. For the whale is indeed wrapped up in his blubber as in a real blanket or bedspread — or, better still, an Indian poncho slipped over his head and hanging down around his extremity. It is because of this cozy blanketing of his body that the whale is able to keep himself comfortable in all weathers, in all seas, times, and tides. What would become of a Greenland whale, say, in those shuddering, icy seas of the North, if he were not supplied with his cozy overcoat? True, other fish are found to be exceedingly lively in those Hyperborean waters; but these, mind you, are your cold-blooded, lungless fish, whose very bellies are refrigerators; creatures that warm themselves in the lee of an iceberg, as a traveler in winter would bask before an inn fire; whereas, like man, the whale has lungs and warm blood. Freeze his blood, and he dies. How wonderful it is, then — unless it is explained — that this great monster, to whom bodily warmth is as indispensable as it is to man; how wonderful that he should be found at home, immersed to his lips for life in those Arctic waters! — where, when seamen fall overboard, they are sometimes found months afterward, frozen upright into the hearts of fields of ice, as a fly is found glued in amber. But it is more surprising still to know, as has been proved by experiment, that the blood of a Polar whale is warmer than that of a Borneo negro in summer.

items.new: In disposing of the body of a right whale, when brought alongside the ship, the same preliminary proceedings commonly take place as in the case of a sperm whale; only, with the sperm whale the head is cut off whole, but with the right whale the lips and tongue are separately removed and hoisted on deck, with all the well-known black bone (the baleen, or whalebone) attached to what is called the crown-piece. But nothing like this, in the present case, had been done. The carcasses of both whales had dropped astern; and the head-laden ship not a little resembled a mule carrying a pair of overburdening panniers.
